headline: High: Langflow’s default server-side file, code, and network surfaces can amplify Authelia-fed inputs into prompt injection, leakage, and cascading action errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Authelia can expose OAuth/ForwardAuth outputs and broad network egress, while Langflow ingests files and chains tools in graph flows. A shared filesystem or copied outputs can let attacker-controlled content from Authelia-adjacent flows be treated as instructions by Langflow. This is plausible in default deployments, though not directly documented as a bridge.
conditions: IF Authelia outputs are copied into Langflow file inputs or flow variables
IF Langflow nodes parse those inputs as instructions or prompts
mitigations: Restrict Langflow inputs to plain data schemas
Add a provenance label to all Authelia-derived content
Disable any node that executes free-form text as instructions
Use separate workspaces for the two systems
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlists at the flow boundary

B_data_leakage.rationale: Authelia handles authentication traffic and has broad network egress; Langflow stores per-flow credentials and reads/writes server filesystem files. If the same workspace or secrets are exposed to both, Langflow can surface intermediate outputs and credentials while Authelia-related data may traverse networked components. The pair creates a realistic leakage path, though the exact shared-data flow is not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents are deployed on the same host or shared volume
IF sensitive flow inputs or credentials are placed into Langflow files or stores
mitigations: Separate storage volumes for each agent
Move secrets out of Langflow stores where possible
Rotate any credentials that were imported into flows
Limit Authelia logs to non-sensitive fields
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data segregation and retention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Authelia has broad network egress, and Langflow can execute shell, install packages, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem. If they share a writable directory or deployment host, Langflow can overwrite artifacts while Authelia serves traffic, creating direct conflict and possible irreversible state corruption. The profiles show overlapping mutable surfaces and no locking mechanism.
conditions: IF both agents share a writable directory or container volume
IF Langflow flows modify files that Authelia reads or serves
mitigations: Place each agent in its own filesystem namespace
Mount Authelia config read-only
Disable Langflow write access to shared paths
Run both under separate service accounts
requires-engineering: add locking around any shared mutable resource

D_cascading_error.rationale: Langflow is a graph-based orchestrator that can chain multiple agents and tools, while Authelia can emit authentication decisions and related outputs. If Langflow treats Authelia-derived outputs as authoritative, it can propagate a mistaken auth or policy result into downstream actions without verification. That creates a default-dangerous cascade with potentially irreversible operational impact.
conditions: IF Langflow uses Authelia outputs as flow inputs without validation
IF downstream nodes take actions based on those outputs
mitigations: Insert a verification step before any action node
Require structured, typed outputs from Authelia
Add human approval for sensitive downstream actions
Log and diff intermediate decisions before execution
requires-engineering: implement policy checks between flow nodes

E_compliance.rationale: Authelia is an authentication service and Langflow stores flow inputs, intermediate outputs, and per-flow credentials. Even without a named residency mismatch, the pair can place sensitive identity and workflow data under different retention and logging regimes. The compliance risk is therefore a policy mismatch on shared data classes, not a proven jurisdictional violation.
conditions: IF authentication logs or flow inputs contain regulated personal data
IF Authelia and Langflow retention or deletion policies differ for the same records
mitigations: Align retention settings across both systems
Minimize identity data stored in flows
Document which system is system-of-record for each data class
Review logs for regulated fields
requires-engineering: implement unified deletion/export handling
